profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential Salt Lake City - Downtown) is located at 572 South Delong St, Suite 100, Salt Lake City, UT 84104. The operator publishes a footprint of 44550 square feet and 2.65 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building, with published certifications and compliance attestations including HITRUST CSF, PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, NIST 800-53, ITAR, SSAE 18. This building is one of six Flexential locations serving the Salt Lake City market. Salt Lake City's data center sector is drawn in part by some of the lowest electricity and natural gas rates in the nation, historically around 5 to 6 cents per kilowatt-hour from a mix of natural gas and renewable generation, a cooling-efficient high-desert climate, and Utah's sales-and-use tax exemption for data center equipment purchases at facilities exceeding 150,000 square feet, retroactive to mid-2016, according to industry market analysis. Seismic activity along the Wasatch Front is a real engineering consideration for the region's data centers, mitigated through structural design. Other major operators active in the broader Salt Lake City market include DataBank in Bluffdale, Aligned Data Centers in West Jordan, Novva Data Centers, QTS in Eagle Mountain, Meta, and Oracle, reflecting the area's shift from smaller retail colocation toward larger enterprise, HPC, and hyperscale capacity.

Flexential itself traces to the 1999 founding of ViaWest, which built out a Western US colocation footprint including Utah before merging with the Southeast-focused Peak 10 in 2017 and rebranding as Flexential in 2018; the company is now privately held with GI Partners as controlling sponsor. Utah's data center water use has drawn growing state scrutiny: a bill from Rep. Jill Koford, advanced unanimously by a legislative water panel in November 2025 for the 2026 session, would require data centers to report annual water consumption to the state under a $10,000-per-day fine for non-compliance, with individual figures kept anonymized publicly but available to state water officials. Reporting on the bill cited examples ranging from facilities using up to 5 million gallons a day, more than 12,000 times a typical household's usage, to the NSA's Bluffdale, Utah facility at about 23 million gallons annually, against low-water designs like Novva's reported 85,000 gallons; Koford said state water regulators had previously been left out of data-center water-use oversight, which had been handled mainly through city permitting.

reading.body:
This building publishes 2.65 MW of critical load UPS capacity across 44,550 square feet in downtown Salt Lake City, one of six Flexential locations serving the metro area. At typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, this translates to roughly 66 racks of accelerator capacity, assuming the full IT load is GPU-intensive, which would make this facility too small for large-model training but sized for inference, smaller models, or traditional enterprise workloads. The published certifications—HITRUST CSF, PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, NIST 800-53, ITAR, SSAE 18—qualify the building to host regulated workloads including federal and financial services work, though the operator does not publish which tenants occupy the space.

Salt Lake City ranks as a secondary US data center hub driven by electricity costs historically around 5 to 6 cents per kilowatt-hour from natural gas and renewable generation, a high-desert climate suited to air cooling, and state sales-and-use tax exemptions for data center equipment at facilities over 150,000 square feet. This facility, at 44,550 square feet, falls below that threshold and does not qualify for the exemption. The region hosts other major operators including DataBank, Aligned Data Centers, Novva, QTS, Meta, and Oracle alongside Flexential's footprint, and seismic activity along the Wasatch Front is a real engineering consideration mitigated through structural design.

In Utah's published data center capacity, this building ranks 6th by MW among the 9 facilities with disclosed figures, which together total 52.18 MW. The state has mapped 21 data center facilities overall, but most publish no capacity numbers. A 2026 legislative bill, advanced unanimously by a water panel in November 2025, would require data centers to report annual water consumption to state regulators, reflecting growing scrutiny of water use in the sector; the bill cites examples ranging from facilities consuming millions of gallons daily to designs using as little as 85,000 gallons annually.
